The Common snipe (Gallinago gallinago) is a medium-sized wader exhibiting a life-history strategy finely tuned to its temperate and subarctic breeding grounds. Eggs are incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], and field data indicate that hatching occurs after approximately 19 days [ab = approximately 19 days]. This incubation period lies within the 17 to 21 day range reported across the species' extensive Holarctic distribution. Upon hatching, precocial chicks emerge with a wet weight at birth of only 11.1 grams [Wwb = 11.1 grams], a relatively low neonatal mass that reflects the considerable yolk investment required to sustain embryonic development under cool spring conditions. This initial body size is modest compared to many other scolopacids, but the downy young are capable of self-feeding within hours, a crucial adaptation for exploiting ephemeral wetland invertebrates. The rapid transition from a yolk-dependent embryo to an exotrophic chick places immediate demands on the chick's thermoregulatory capabilities, as the typical nest microclimate around 36 °C [T = 36 °C] is soon exchanged for the variable conditions of the fen or marsh edge.

Under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species, approximately 41 °C [T = 41 °C], a predictable sequence of developmental and reproductive milestones unfolds. Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight and departure from the nest vicinity, occurs at 19.5 days after hatching [tx = 19.5 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. This relatively short fledgling period—consistent with the 19 to 20 day range given in handbooks—is characteristic of many ground-nesting waders that must attain flight capability quickly to evade terrestrial predators. Following fledging, juveniles continue to refine their foraging skills while remaining dependent on parental vigilance for several weeks. The pace of subsequent somatic growth is rapid, driven by a diet dominated by earthworms, Diptera larvae, and other soil macroinvertebrates. By the time of autumn migration, first-year birds approach adult dimensions, setting the stage for the physiological processes of sexual maturation that will occur over the ensuing months.

Sexual maturation in Gallinago gallinago is attained at 58.5 days after hatching [tp = 58.5 days after hatching], a value derived from captive-reared birds maintained at 41 °C [T = 41 °C] during the post-fledging period. This surprisingly early onset of gonadal development does not translate into immediate breeding, as time since birth at first brood is deferred until 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. The prolonged interval between sexual maturity and actual reproduction is ecologically meaningful: young birds must first complete their first pre-basic moult, accumulate sufficient fat reserves for migration, and, upon returning to breeding grounds, establish a territory and secure a mate. This life-history pattern—where puberty precedes first breeding by many months—is widespread among long-distance migratory waders and reflects the severe constraints on time and energy imposed by a short Arctic or boreal summer. First-year birds that delay breeding until their second calendar year tend to exhibit higher nesting success than those attempting to breed as yearlings.

The maximum lifespan recorded for the Common snipe under natural conditions is approximately 9.2 years [am = approximately 9.2 years], with the oldest confirmed individuals approaching a decade of age at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. Longevity data, assembled from ringing recoveries across Europe, indicate that adult survival is relatively high for a bird of its body size, a life-history feature often associated with species that experience low annual reproductive output. Field studies of reproductive output show that females lay between 2 and 5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 2 and 5 eggs per clutch], with only a single clutch produced each year [F_R_i = single clutch produced each year], yielding a maximum reproduction rate of approximately 0.01 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 0.01 eggs per day]. This modest fecundity—combined with occasional replacement clutches following early nest loss—yields a maximum annual recruitment that is limited by the brevity of the breeding season. The combination of a single annual nesting attempt and moderate clutch size means that population persistence is heavily dependent on high adult survivorship, particularly among established breeding adults in optimal wetland habitats.

Adult body mass varies substantially between the sexes, with the ultimate wet weight of adult males averaging approximately 94 grams [Wwi = approximately 94 grams], while females attain a larger ultimate wet weight of 111 grams [Wwi = 111 grams]. This sexual size dimorphism, in which females are roughly 15-20% heavier than males, is typical among many scolopacid waders and is commonly interpreted as an adaptation to the energetic demands of egg production and incubation. The species' recorded adult mass range of 80 to 140 grams broadly overlaps with these sex-specific means, though individual variation is strongly influenced by seasonal fat loads accumulated before long-distance migration. Under the metabolic conditions characteristic of an active bird at 41 °C [T = 41 °C], the daily energy expenditure of a 100-gram snipe is considerable, necessitating near-continuous foraging during both diurnal and nocturnal periods. The ability to deposit and mobilise substantial lipid reserves is central to the species' capacity to breed successfully in high-latitude wetlands and then undertake transcontinental migrations to wintering grounds across Europe, Africa, and South Asia.
